The Hanuman Chalisa contains forty main verses, with two opening couplets and one closing couplet.
The Chalisa is traditionally attributed to Goswami Tulsidas and written in a language closely connected to everyday speech in his region.
Strength, wisdom and knowledge. The prayer brings physical courage and inner understanding together.
The opening uses the image of cleaning a mirror to describe preparing the mind through the guru’s guidance.
The first verse calls him an ocean of wisdom and virtue. His immense strength is praised in the next.
One reading can be your daily prayer.
The Chalisa does not set a minimum of three, seven or eleven readings. A single attentive recitation can be a meaningful devotional practice.
These counts may be chosen for a personal prayer commitment or followed within a tradition. The Chalisa does not assign a separate, guaranteed benefit to each.
Verse 38 associates a hundred readings with freedom from bondage and great happiness. It does not say they must all happen in one sitting.
Reflect on one verse at a time.
Each verse offers something to contemplate, from courage to service. Calling every verse a “maha mantra” expresses devotional reverence; it is not a classification given by the Chalisa itself.
Verse 26 connects remembering Hanuman with all three, inviting prayer to influence everyday life.
It ends with Hanuman in the heart.
The closing prayer welcomes Hanuman together with Rama, Sita and Lakshmana.
A fruit as bright as the sun.
A beloved childhood story describes him reaching for the sun, thinking it was something delicious to eat. The Chalisa recalls this episode.
Anjaneya refers to his mother Anjana, while Pavanputra means son of the wind. The Chalisa also calls him Kesari’s son.
Sacred stories describe him becoming tiny or enormous as the task required. The Chalisa remembers his different forms.
In the Ramayana, the ring helps Sita recognise him as Rama’s messenger when he finds her in Lanka.
Across the ocean on a rescue.
His famous leap to Lanka was part of the search for Sita, a feat of strength in the service of someone else.
In the familiar Ramayana account, he brings the mountain when he cannot identify the needed herb, helping save Lakshmana.
The Chalisa recalls Rama telling Hanuman that he is as dear to him as Bharata.
He brought Rama and Sugriva together.
He plays an important role in their alliance, showing his ability to build trust as well as overcome obstacles.
He loves to hear Rama’s story.
The Chalisa describes his love of listening to Rama’s deeds, with Rama, Sita and Lakshmana living in his heart.
The Chalisa celebrates his extraordinary abilities while describing him as Rama’s devoted servant. A lesson we can draw is to use our abilities with care and purpose.
